text: Atmospheric methane isotopic record favors fossil sources flat in 1980s and 1990s with recent increase
Andrew L. Ricea12, Christopher L. Butenhoffa1, Doaa G. Teama, Florian H. Rogera,M.Aslam K. Khalila, and Reinhold A. Rasmussenb

Observations of atmospheric methane $( C H _ { 4 } )$ since the late 1970s and measurements of $\mathsf { C H } _ { 4 }$ trapped in ice and snow reveal a meteoric rise in concentration during much of the twentieth century. Since 1750, levels of atmospheric $\mathsf { C H } _ { 4 }$ have more than doubled to current globally averaged concentration near 1,80o ppb. During the late 1980s and 1990s, the $\mathsf { C H } _ { 4 }$ growth rate slowed substantially and was near or at zero between 1999 and 2006. There is no scientific consensus on the drivers of this slowdown. Here,we report measurements of the stable isotopic composition of atmospheric $\mathsf { C H } _ { 4 }$ ${ ( ^ { 1 3 } \mathsf { C } I ^ { 1 2 } \mathsf { C } }$ and D/H) from a rare air archive dating from 1977 to 1998.Together with more modern records of isotopic atmospheric $C H _ { 4 } ,$ we performed a time-dependent retrieval of methane fluxes spanning $_ { 2 5 \mathrm { ~ y ~ } }$ (1984-2o09) using a 3D chemical transport model. This inversion results in a 24[18,27]Tg $\mathbf { y } ^ { - 1 } \mathsf { C H } _ { 4 }$ increase in fugitive fossil fuel emissions since 1984 with most of this growth occurring after year 20oo. This result is consistent with some bottom-up emissions inventories but not with recent estimates based on atmospheric ethane.In fact,when forced with decreasing emissions from fossil fuel sources our inversion estimates unreasonably high emissions in other sources. Further, the inversion estimates a decrease in biomass-burning emissions that could explain falling ethane abundance.A range of sensitivity tests suggests that these results are robust.

However, disagreement remains over the magnitudes and, importantly, the trends in $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ source categories during this period of atmospheric growth rate decline.In particular，two recent studies using the tracer ethane have linked a sustained drop in ethane mixing ratios to a decrease in fugitive fossil fuel-based $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ emissions by $\mathbf { \bar { 1 0 } } \mathbf { - } 3 0 \ \mathrm { T g } \ \mathbf { y } ^ { - 1 }$ since the 1980s (6,7). This top-down result differs with bottom-up emissions inventories that show increasing or flat fugitive fossil fuel $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ emissions (8). Contemporaneously,other work (9) used trends in the interhemispheric gradient in the carbon isotopic composition $( \delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C } )$ of $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ to infer that biogenic $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ sources of $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ declined over the period 1984- 2005,which authors link to ${ \sim } 1 6 \mathrm { T g y ^ { - 1 } }$ decrease in rice agricultural emissions. This agrees with several bottom-up studies (10,11). However,this claim was challenged by an analysis of new and existing $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C }$ of $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ results that do not show such a trend (12). A synthesis of available information seems to favor“decreasing-tostable"fugitive fossil fuel $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ sources during the 1980s and 1990s (3),a conclusion that is supported by a very recent box-model analysis (13).What is noteworthy,however, is that in either case of fossil or rice sources,a long-term decrease in one source category would require an increase in another to balance the total global $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ budget over the period.

Significance

There is no scientific consensus on the drivers of the atmospheric methane growth rate over the past three decades. Here, we report carbon and hydrogen isotopic measurements of atmospheric methane in archived air samples collected 1977-1998, and modeling of these with more contemporary data to infer changes in methane sources over the period 1984-2009. We present strong evidence that methane emissions from fossil fuel sectors were approximately constant in the 1980s and 1990s but increased significantly between 2000 and 2009. This finding challenges recent conclusions based on atmospheric ethane that fugitive fossil fuel emissions fell during much of this period. Emissions from other anthropogenic sources also increased, but were partially offset by reductions in wetland and fire emissions.

Isotopic information is particularly useful as a direct means to constrain and to interpret temporal changes in the $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ budget due to characteristic isotope ratios in major $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ sources: wetlands, rice and ruminant emissions $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C } \sim - 6 0 \% o$ $8 D \sim - 3 0 0 \text{‰}$ ； fugitive fossil fuel emissions $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C } \sim - 4 0 \% o$ $8 \mathrm { D } \sim - 1 7 5 \% o$ ; biomass-burning emissions $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C } \sim - 2 0 \% o$ 8D\~ $- 20 \text{‰}$ (SI Ap-pendix, Table S1). Despite the promise of isotopic $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ to help constrain the $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ budget, the scientific community is historically data limited; before ${ \sim } 1 9 9 8 $ there were few isotopic $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ time series available and none that spanned decadal lengths (12, $1 4 -$ 17). This is particularly true for δD,for which very little data are available at all before the turn of the century.

To fill this void,we analyzed a rare archive of more than 200 air samples collected at Cape Meares, Oregon (CM; $4 5 . 5 \mathrm { ^ \circ N }$ ， $1 2 4 . 0 ^ { \circ } \dot { \mathbf W } )$ between 1977 and i998 to examine trends in the dualtracer isotopic composition ( $\mathrm { 8 ^ { 1 3 } C }$ and δD) of atmospheric $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ An additional 1oo archive samples measured were from sites including: Mauna Loa $( 2 1 . 1 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { N }$ ， $\mathrm { \bar { 1 5 7 . 2 ^ { \circ } W } ) }$ and Cape Kumukahi $ \bf ( 1 9 . 3 \%$ ， $1 5 4 . 5 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { W }$ ,Hawaii (1992-1996)； Tutuila,American Samoa $( 1 4 . 1 \mathrm { { ^ \circ S } }$ ， $1 7 0 . 6 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { W }$ ,1995)； South Pole $( 9 0 ^ { \circ } \mathbf { S }$ ,1992-1995); and Sable Island,Nova Scotia $( 4 3 . 9 \mathrm { ^ \circ N }$ ， $6 0 . 0 2 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { W }$ ,1992).

To infer changes in the $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ budget for the years 1984-2009 we used the chemical transport model GEOS-Chem (18) at $4 ^ { \circ } \times$ $5 ^ { \circ }$ spatial resolution and performed a Bayesian inversion of atmospheric observations of $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ mixing ratio using monthly $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ mixing ratios at 221 sites from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Earth System Research Laboratory GLOBALVIEW-CH4 data product (19) and $8 ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C }$ from several observational networks including the current work, the Institute of Arctic and Alpine Research (2O), Quay et al. (16),and Tyler et al. (17).
Results

Three-Decade Record of Isotopic $\mathbf { C H } _ { 4 }$ .The resulting isotopic measurements at CM constitute one of the longest continuous records of the isotopic composition of methane and date back to a time when no other time series data are available (late 1970s and early 198Os). This is an important time for understanding the $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ budget, as the $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ growth rate is in a sustained multidecadal decline.To create a more than three-decade uninterrupted record of isotopic $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ ，which extends to near-present time,we combine historic $8 ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C }$ data from CM with published datasets from midlatitude North America from Olympic Peninsula,Washington (CPO; $4 8 \mathrm { { ^ \circ N } }$ ， $1 2 6 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { W }$ ,1988-1996; ref. 16),Montana de Oro, California (MDO; $3 5 \mathrm { { ^ \circ N } }$ ， $1 2 1 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { { W } }$ ,1996-2006; ref.17) and Niwot Ridge, Colorado (NWR; $4 0 \%$ ， $1 0 5 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { W }$ ,1994-2010; refs.15,17). The 8D time series from CM were combined with existing data from MDO and NWR (2000-2006; ref.17). These locations were found to have comparable behavior in their seasonal cycles and long-term trends over periods of overlap.Because absolute values in concentration, $8 ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C }$ and 8D vary spatially, mean values were adjusted using periods of overlap between datasets (SI Appendix, section S.2). This approach also accounts for small adjustments resulting from calibration differences between laboratories,found to be critical in previous work (12). Together with the long-standing $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ concentration record, this composite record from the midlatitude Northern Hemisphere provides a record of the secular and seasonal trends in isotopic $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ as well as some of the interannual variability (Fig.1).

This composite Northern Hemisphere record captures the slowdown of the $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ growth rate, well-characterized over the past three decades (Fig. $1 A$ and $D$ ).Decadally averaged growth rates were found to be within the range of NOAA,Advanced Global Atmospheric Gases Experiment (AGAGE),University of California, Irvine (UCI),and Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organization (CSIRO) historical records (3), $1 5 . 1 \pm 4 . 0$ $( \pm 9 5 \%$ CI) ppb $\mathbf { y } ^ { - 1 }$ during the 1980s, $6 . 1 \pm 2 . 3 \mathrm { p p b y } ^ { - 1 }$ during the 1990s, and $3 . 5 \pm 1 . 1$ ppb $\mathbf { \bar { y } } ^ { - 1 }$ during the 2000s $( 2 . 7 \dot { \pm } 1 . 0 \mathrm { p p } \dot { \bf b } \mathrm { \bf y } ^ { - 1 }$ 2000-2006; $4 . 6 \pm 1 . 3 \mathrm { \ p p b { \dot { y } } ^ { - 1 } }$ ,2006-2010). The agreement between this composite midlatitude Northern Hemisphere dataset and the global mean derived from global monitoring datasets is due to the long lifetime of $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ in the atmosphere $( \sim 9 ~ \mathrm { y } )$ and resulting low spatial variability.Interannual variability in the $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ growth rate is also captured in most years, compatible with the NOAA global network (21) (Fig. 1 $D ; { \dot { r } } ^ { 2 } = { \dot { 0 } } . 6 4$ ).

The consistency between $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ time series from these composite $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ data and global networks provides confidence that observed temporal trends in the time series from the composite $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ isotope dataset reflect global trends rather than regional ones. Both $8 ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C }$ and SD isotopic datasets show distinct behavior from $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ mixing ratio (Fig. $1 B$ and $C$ ).Beginning near $- 4 7 . 7 \text{‰}$ and $- 1 1 0 \text{‰}$ in the late 1970s, $8 ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C }$ and δD increase with mean trends of $0 . 0 2 1 \pm 0 . 0 1 9 \% o$ and $0 . 5 9 \pm 0 . 2 8 \% o \mathrm { \ y } ^ { - 1 }$ respectively $( \pm 9 5 \% \mathrm { C I } )$ in the 1980s and $0 . 0 2 2 \pm 0 . 0 2 7 \% o$ and $1 . 0 2 \pm 0 . \dot { 2 } 4 \% o \mathrm { y } ^ { - 1 }$ in the 1990s (Fig. $1 E$ and $F$ ).Maximum values of $8 ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C }$ and 8D of $47 . 2 \text{‰}$ and $95 \text{‰}$ are reached in the early 2OoOs followed by a leveling off or slight decrease in both isotopic tracers during the 2000-20o5 period, which experienced a general stabilization of $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ mixing ratios.The rate of change in $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \dot { \mathrm { C } }$ and 8D after the year 2000 averaged $- 0 . 0 1 \pm 0 . 0 2 9 \% o { \bf y } ^ { - 1 }$ (2000-2010) and $- 0 . 2 \pm 1 . 4 \% o \mathbf { y } ^ { - 1 }$ (2000-2006),respectively.

Model Inversions. The match between optimized-model (a posteriori) and observations of $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ concentration and $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C }$ for all fixed sites is shown in $S I$ Appendix, Fig. S2. The paucity of historical SD measurements limited its utility as a source constraint and SD was withheld from model inversions in favor of an additional a posteriori model validation ( $S I$ Appendix, Fig. S3). The effects of a wide array of more than 5O sensitivity tests (SI Appendix, Table S4) provides an assessment of uncertainty of inferred mean annual source fluxes (SI Appendix, Table S1) and in temporal trends of sources $S I$ Appendix, Fig. S4). Sensitivity scenarios did change mean annual flux strengths in the $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ budget as perturbations to the base scenario require source flux adjustments to rebalance both the total and isotopic budgets( $S I$ Appendix, Table S1).This is most evident when we perturbed both the isotopic fractionation of atmospheric $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ and the total $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ budget by altering sink processes. For example the addition of an isotopically fractioning marine boundary layer chlorine sink (SI Appendix, scenario S6.1） reduced emissions from the isotopically enriched biomass-burning source $( - 2 0 \mathrm { T g \ y ^ { - 1 } } )$ and increased emissions from the isotopically depleted biogenic source $( + 4 0 \mathrm { ~ T g ~ y ~ } ^ { - 1 } )$ ). The opposite effect was true when we decreased the kinetic isotope effect of the OH sink (SI Appendix, scenario S7, see SI Appendix section S.6 for details). However, the effect of most sensitivity scenarios on decadal-scale trends inferred from the data is minimal and the results of the base case appear robust (Fig. 2, $S I$ Appendix, Fig. S4). Further, trends inferred in broader source categories with similar isotopic composition (e.g., all biogenic emissions） show smaller ranges than for individual source categories (SI Appendix, Fig. S4).

Results of the inversion analysis indicate the emission rate of anthropogenic sources (not including biomass burning) increased by 40 [16, 62] $\mathrm { T g } \mathrm { y } ^ { - 1 }$ (range given for $1 0 \mathrm { { t h } }$ and 90th percentiles of sensitivity analyses) over the $2 5 \mathrm { - y }$ study period,with significant increases in fugitive fossil fuel (24 [18,27] $\mathrm { T g \ y ^ { - 1 } } .$ )，ruminant livestock $( 9 [ 4 , \breve { 1 } 4 ] \mathrm { T g } \mathrm { y } ^ { - 1 } . \nonumber$ ),and waste management emissions (19 [15,25] $\mathrm { T g ~ y ^ { - 1 } }$ ).Wetlands were the largest contributor to interannual variations in $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ emissions and growth rate (Fig. 2). Within this variability,litle change is inferred in the secular trend of the wetland source 1984-2000 (6 [-4,11] $\mathrm { T g \ y ^ { - 1 } }$ increase). However, the following_decade (2000-2009) experienced a significant decrease (29 [25, 32] $\mathrm { T g ~ y ^ { - 1 } }$ ）in wetland $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ emissions continuing a trend inferred by Bousquet et al. (22).We find that rice emissions,although highly variable,do decrease significantly $( 1 2 \left[ 8 , 1 7 \right] \mathrm { T g } \mathrm { y } ^ { - 1 }$ ;Fig. $2 F .$ )over the entire modeled period 1984 2009,consistent with bottom-up assessments (i0,11). The contribution of biomass-burning emissions toward interannual variability is minor except during the 1997-1998 anomaly in good agreement with previous top-down constraints but differing from bottom-up estimates,which tend to emphasize its role (3). However,excluding this large anomaly we find decreasing emis-sions from biomass burning of 14 [12, 18] $\mathrm { T g } \mathrm { y } ^ { - 1 }$ over the period 1984-20o9.Although there is no consensus from bottom-up fire inventories on the long-term trends in $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ emissions from biomass burning (23),we note evidence of decreasing burned area from fires in recent decades, supportive of this result (24, 25). Initially higher than the priors during the mid 198Os,combined fugitive fossil fuel $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ emissions (natural gas,oil, and coal) are flat during the period 1984-2000 consistent in trend with Emissions Database for Global Atmospheric Research (EDGAR) emissions inventories $( 4 \left[ - 5 , 5 \right] \mathrm { T g } \mathrm { y } ^ { - 1 } .$ ).Subsequent to 20o0,fugitive fossil fuel emissions increased by 21 [15,24] $\mathrm { T g } \mathrm { y } ^ { - 1 }$ over the next $9 { \bf y }$ Further, inversion results indicate growth in natural gas and oil sectors over the entire modeled period 1984-2009 (21[16, 24] $\mathrm { T g } \mathrm { y } ^ { - 1 }$ increase) contrasted by coal, which experienced a decrease in the 1980s followed by a leveling ofin the 1990s (7 [5,10] $\mathrm { T g } \mathrm { y } ^ { - 1 }$ decrease, 1984- 2000) and a small increase in the 2000s (5 [4,7] $\mathrm { T g ~ y ^ { - 1 } }$ increase, 2000-2009). Both recent increases in coal emissions,from increased mining in China,and increased natural gas emissions,from the onset of large-scale hydraulic fracturing of shale gas,are substantiated by recent studies and emissons inventories (8, 21,26). Early in the 2OoOs,a coincident strong decrease in wetland emissions keeps total $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ emissions stable,but the end of this trend combined with growing emissions from livestock,waste,and fossil fuel industry lead to an uptick in the global $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ sources after 2005.

Optimized forward model results (using base scenario emissions derived from $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ and $8 ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C }$ observations) for CM, MDO, and NWR for SD (Fig.1C) provide a final assessment of model bias.Seasonality and secular trend are well matched with the composite northern hemispheric dataset for the majority of the observational period (SI Appendix,Fig. S3)， illustrating that the model simulations represent withheld data well overall. However, there is some discrepancy in the last $2 { \mathrm { ~ y ~ } }$ of the time series where observations of SD level off yet modeled δD continues to rise.This contrasts optimized modeled $8 ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C }$ ，which shows a leveling off during this period consistent with observations.The mismatch of modeled δD late in the time series may be in part due to the assigned SD isotopic signatures of sources (SI Appendix, Table S1), which are more poorly constrained than $\mathring { 8 } ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C }$ Modeling sensitivity studies that decreased the isotopic signatures (δD) of $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ sources (wetlands, biomass-burning,and fossil fuel emissions) reproduced the SD trend late in the time series; however, these model runs resulted in a decrease in the match with observations overall by decreasing modeled 8D isotopic composition over the entire period ( $S I$ Appendix, Fig. S5).
Discussion

Comparison of Model Inversion with Prior Studies. Consistent with earlier work and a recent synthesis that calculates the global $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ source at $5 5 1 ~ \mathrm { T g ~ y } ^ { - 1 }$ 1980-1989, $5 5 4 ~ \mathrm { T g ~ y } ^ { - 1 }$ 1990-1999,and $5 4 8 \mathrm { T g } \mathrm { y } ^ { - 1 } 2 0 0 0 { - } 2 \breve { 0 } 0 \breve { 9 }$ (3), the composite northern hemispheric middle latitude methane concentration dataset (Fig. $1 A$ and $D$ showing an exponential decay in the $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ growth rate） and our global model inversion is broadly consistent with substantial interannual variability but absence of any substantial secular trend in the total global $\mathrm { C } \mathrm { H } _ { 4 }$ source over the past three decades (through 2OO6). It is telling,however, that the secular trends observed in isotopic $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ do not show a similar asymptotic behavior and fall below trends toward steady-state equilibrium indicating a shift among sources within a roughly constant global total.A simple time-dependent mass-balance approach based on observed $8 ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C }$ and SD and their trends in time (Fig.1) indicates that source isotopic composition was in decline Over the period 1978-2009 $( \delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C } \sim \dot { 0 } . 3 \% o$ ， $\bar { \mathrm {8 D } } { \sim } 3 \% o$ ； $S I$ Appendix, Fig. S6). This result is supported by the full global model inversion, which also infersa falling global mean $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C }$ of emissions of the same rate (1984-2009; SI Appendix, Fig. S6). These isotopic trends are qualitatively consistent with some changes in the $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ budget over the three-decade period,specifically relative decreases in one or more isotopically enriched sources (i.e., fossil fuel or biomass burning） and relative increases in isotopically depleted sources (i.e.,natural wetlands,agricultural or waste; SI Appendix, Table S1) keep global emissions roughly constant.

There is independent evidence in studies for declines in both $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ emissions from global biomass-burning (25) and fugitive fossil fuel emissions (27) over the past few decades.However, there is disagreement on this topic and other studies infer increasing trends in these sources (8,28). Global-scale model inversion results presented here favor a decrease in fire $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ emissions due in part to leverage on the isotopic budget of $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ resulting from their enriched $8 ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C }$ signature (SI Appendix, Table S1), i.e., a change in fire emissions will result in a larger shift in $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C }$ than an equivalent change in fugitive fossil fuel emissions.Predominantly located in the tropics,a global decrease in biomass-burning emissions also has little impact on the meridional distribution of $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$

Of isotopically depleted sources,natural wetlands are the largest source at ${ \bf \tilde { \Omega } } { \bf \Omega } { \sim } 1 6 5 { \bf \Omega } \mathrm { T g \Omega y } ^ { - 1 }$ . Some bottom-up studies indicate upward decadal-scale trends in global wetland emissions (29), but top-down estimates using ground-based observations and satellite-based products combined with atmospheric models tend to favor constant or declining wetland emissions over the past few decades (3),consistent with this work. Global $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ emissions from solid waste are generally considered to have increased over the past few decades from increases in landfilled solid waste, even as $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ recovery increased (8,3O).Emissions from ruminant animals are also generally recognized to have risen over the past few decades due to increased populations of livestock (8, 31).Increases in both waste emissions and livestock emissions, which contribute to observed trends in $8 ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C }$ and δD, are supported by inversion results here over the 1984-2009 period (i9 [15, 25] and 9 [4, 15] $\mathrm { T g ~ y ^ { - 1 } }$ respectively; Fig. $2 C$ and $D$ ).

Finally, several bottom-up emissions inventories indicate a significant decrease in rice $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ emissions in recent decades (10,11). This result is corroborated by inversion results here,which show a decrease in rice emissions (12 [8,17] $\mathrm { T g ~ y ^ { - 1 } }$ decrease over the period 1984-2009;Fig. $2 F$ .Although rice emissions are isotopically depleted,and a decrease in rice emissions alone would increase the average global source $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C }$ ，modeling results suggest that this change is offset by increasing emissions from waste and livestock categories and decreasing emissions from biomass burning.Notably,a decrease in rice emissions is inferred by our model without a significant change in the interhemispheric gradient in $8 ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C }$ and 8D (SI Appendix, Fig. S7), consistent with Levin et al. (12). An interhemispheric gradient observed in $8 ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C }$ was proposed by Kai et al.(9) as evidence of a decrease in global rice emissions. Based on our analyses,either the decrease in rice emissions is masked by concomitant increases in waste and livestock categories or the interhemispheric gradient in $8 ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C }$ is somewhat insensitive to changes in rice emissions,which are primarily at low latitudes (8).

Clearly some unresolved differences remain between approaches that assess changes in the $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ budget over the past few decades.It is particularly difficult to reconcile the results here with the assertion of decreasing $( 1 0 { - } 3 0 \mathrm { T g \ y ^ { - 1 } } \mathrm { . }$ ）natural gas and oil fugitive emissions based on falling ethane mixing ratios (6, 7). This scenario was selected as more likely than decreasing microbial emissions to explain the stabilization of $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ emissions in arecent review synthesis (3).To further investigate this hy-pothesis, we tested two scenarios based on falling ethane mixing ratios [storyline $\mathbf { S } _ { 1 }$ and $\mathbf { S ^ { \prime } } _ { 1 }$ from Kirschke et al. (3)]. They first fixed gas and oil fugitive $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ emissions to the scheme derived from the ethane dataset requiring a decrease of $1 8 \ \mathrm { T g \ y ^ { - 1 } }$ over the period 1985-2000,increasing $\overline { { 2 } } \mathrm { T g } \mathrm { y } ^ { - 1 }$ over the period $2 0 0 0 -$ 2009 (a decrease of ${ \sim } 4 0 \mathrm { T g } \mathrm { y } ^ { - 1 }$ from our modeled base case over the entire period).This forcing of our model inversion resulted in a increase in coal fugitive emissions of ${ \sim } 2 0 ~ \mathrm { T g ~ y } ^ { - 1 }$ over the base case (Fig. $2 B$ ， ${ \sim } 5 0 \%$ rise in coal emissions)and an increase from landfills and waste treatment of ${ \sim } 2 5 \ \mathrm { T g \ s ^ { - 1 } }$ over the base case (Fig. $2 D$ ， ${ > } 5 0 \%$ increase in source） for the entire period (1984-20o9). Both fugitive emissions from coal mining and waste emissions (EDGAR 4.2) have a similar meridional distribution to fugitive natural gas emissions,and the combination of the two maintains the source $8 ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C }$ isotopic composition.In this scenario, small additional changes are also inferred in rice emissions, biomass-burning emissions,livestock emissions,and wetland emissions that satisfy mass balance (Fig.2).Large increases in coal and waste emissions are outliers in emissions inventories and on the high-end of sensitivity tests (Fig. $2 \ B$ and $D$ ).The combination of decreasing natural gas and oil emissions in this scenario and increasing coal emissions results in nearly unchanged fugitive fossil fuel emissions over the period 1984-2009. With both fugitive $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ and ethane emissions occurring in coal mining,this scenario is unlikely to help explain the drop in ethane abundance over the period (6, 7).

Second, noting the incompatibility of increasing fugitive ethane (and $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ ) emissions in coal mining with the ethane record, we apportioned the $1 8 ~ \mathrm { T g ~ y ^ { - 1 } }$ decrease in fugitive emissions between the two fossil fuel categories over the period 1985-2000 followed by a $2 ~ \mathrm { T g ~ y } ^ { - 1 }$ rise (2000-2009)；this scenario is still compatible with storylines $\mathbf { S } _ { 1 }$ and $\mathbf { S ^ { \prime } } _ { 1 }$ from Kirschke et al. (3) (a decrease of ${ \sim } 4 0 \ T \mathrm { g \ i ^ { - 1 } }$ compared with our base-case inversion). Under this scenario,the inversion response was to apportion an increase of ${ \sim } 3 5 \mathrm { T g } \mathrm { { y } ^ { - 1 } }$ into waste and landfill $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ emissions over the base case (Fig. $2 D$ ； ${ \sim } 1 0 0 \%$ increase in source), a ${ \sim } 2 0 ~ \mathrm { T g ~ y } ^ { - 1 }$ increase in biomass burning over the base case (Fig. $2 E$ and $F$ ； ${ \sim } 4 0 \%$ increase in source) and a decrease in wetland and rice emissions $( \sim 1 5 \mathrm { T g } \mathrm { y } ^ { - 1 } )$ from the base case (Fig.2).In this scenario,waste emissions maintain the source meridional distribution,and biomass-burning emissions balance the $\delta ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C }$ flux. Although mathematically possible within the ${ \sim } 5 0 0 \mathrm { T g } \mathrm { y } ^ { - 1 } \mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ budget, there is litte bottom-up support for the required rapid rise in waste and landfill $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ emissions (3).

Without falling fugitive fossil fuel emissions is it possible to explain falling atmospheric ethane abundance? Notably, our baseinversion result of declining biomass-burning emissions could satisfy $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ ,isotopic $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ ,and ethane trends over the period 1984-2009 (Fig. 3). Specifically,applying a calculated $1 4 ~ \mathrm { { \dot { T g } } ~ y ^ { - 1 } }$ decline in biomass-burning $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ emissions from our base inversion and a weighted mean $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ to ethane ratio in fire of 5:1 (32) results in a $3 \mathrm { \check { T } g y ^ { - 1 } }$ decrease in ethane emissions compatible with the observed decrease in atmospheric ethane abundance (7). However, we note that emitted $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ -to-ethane ratiosare variable and better knowledge of global average $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ -to-ethane ratios in fugitive emissions by gas,oil,and coal subsectors and in biomassburning emissions would be particularly helpful in resolving this issue further.

Implications. Overall, we emphasize that although the $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ growth rate went through a dramatic decline over the past three decades,a decline in $\mathrm { \bar { C } H _ { 4 } }$ sources is not needed to balance sources and sinks (5).Nonetheless,there is evidence that source apportionment shifted during this period,which fundamentally requires that a secular change in one source category must be met by a change in equal magnitude and opposite sign in other sources. Global observations of $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ concentration, including its trends and spatial distribution,and trends in $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ isotopic composition ( $\mathrm { 8 ^ { 1 3 } C }$ and δD) provide a top-down constraint to our understanding of how $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ sources have changed over the past three decades.Accordingly,3D global chemical transport models fully use these components and are most useful in the endeavor to best match sources with observations.

text: The Bayesian inversion performed here using the Goddard Earth Observing System (GEOS)-Chem global chemical transport model demonstrates the utility of long-term isotopic measurement records together with long-standing measurements of $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ concentration toward constraining changes in the budget of $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ . This capacity will increase with current and future isotopic observations.Our work here focuses on the period 1984-2009, and finds a significant increase in the anthropogenic source of $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ from 2000,despite being mainly flat in the 198Os and 1990s. $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ interannual variability is dominated by wetland emissions, which show very litle long-term changes through 2Ooo,but decrease after 2Ooo,in agreement with previous work on the subject (22). Further, our measurement-modeling approach favors a scenario of declining rice emissions over the period 1984-2000, as proposed previously (9),but challenged based on the interhemispheric gradient in $\mathrm { \Delta } ^ { \mathrm { \prime 1 3 } } \mathrm { C }$ (12).We find a scenario of decreasing fugitive fossil fuel emissions from 1984 to 2000 unlikely within the observational constraint without a substantial increase in landfill and waste $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 }$ emissions.Finally,our study finds a decline in global biomass-burning emissions (excluding 1997- 1998)over the nearly three-decade period.This result can explain declining global ethane abundance over the period 1984-2000 with roughly constant fugitive fossil fuel emissions.
Methods

Air Archive.Samples analyzed in this work were aliquots of historicair samples obtained from the Oregon Health and Sciences University Division of Environmental and Biomolecular Systems (Sl Appendix,section S.1).
